source: Hartanto et al. (2024) The Effect of Mere Presence of Smartphone on Cognitive Functions: A Four-Level Meta-Analysis
finding: Mere presence of a phone had no overall effect on cognition. Not moderated by phone dependency, FoMO, age, gender, or how presence was manipulated.
numbers: 166 effect sizes, 53 samples, 33 studies, 4,368 participants. Overall d=-0.02, SE=0.02, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.01], p=.246. No significant heterogeneity (tau2=0.00 at all three levels).
quote: mere presence of smartphone had no significant effect on cognitive outcomes
limits: Studies up to the search date only. Most outcomes are one-off tasks; only OSPAN had enough data for its own model.
agent_relevance: Settles gap 4 against brain drain as a general effect. Human-offloading cost from mere presence should not drive agent design.

source: Hartanto et al. (2024) four-level meta-analysis, OSPAN and publication-bias subanalysis
finding: Only the operation-span task (Ward 2017's main measure) showed a small negative effect, and that one looks like publication bias.
numbers: OSPAN: 22 effect sizes, 20 samples, 8 studies, d=-0.13, SE=0.06, 95% CI [-0.25,-0.02], p=.023. Egger b=-1.38, SE=0.69, p=.045 (asymmetric funnel). Bias-adjusted d=-0.04, p=.580.
limits: Egger adjustment on 20 samples is itself imprecise. Authors report no publication-bias or record-type effect in the all-task model.
agent_relevance: The one task behind the original headline is the weakest link. A tool-in-view effect on a working-memory measure is not established.

source: Boettger, Poschik and Zierer (2023) Does the Brain Drain Effect Really Exist? A Meta-Analysis
finding: Pooled small negative effect of smartphone use or presence on cognition, driven by memory outcomes and Asian samples. Heterogeneous.
limits: Pools use and presence, so it does not isolate Ward's claim. Smaller study set, no bias correction seen. Disagrees with Hartanto 2024 (d=-0.02).
agent_relevance: Two meta-analyses disagree: the pooled value is between 0 and -0.14 depending on inclusion rules. Treat as at most small; K16 stays contested.

source: Search summary of Parry (2024) meta-analysis and Ruiz Pardo and Minda (2022) replication of Ward et al. (2017)
finding: Search summary says a 56-study meta-analysis found working memory capacity hurt by mere presence while other functions were null, with heterogeneity and low power. The Ruiz Pardo and Minda direct replication of Ward Exp 2 found no difference on o-span or go/no-go.
numbers: 56 studies (per summary). Pooled value not read.
limits: Snippet only. Do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Another unread meta-analysis; confirms the picture is mixed, nothing to build on.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS 122(26)
finding: Field experiment in Turkish high schools. An unrestricted GPT-4 tutor raised practice scores but lowered later exam scores. A tutor with hints and teacher notes removed the harm but did not beat control.
numbers: Nearly 1,000 students. Practice: GPT Base +48%, GPT Tutor +127% vs control. Exam with AI removed: GPT Base -17% vs control; GPT Tutor about equal to control. Most Base users just asked for the answer.
limits: I read only the Wharton summary page (PNAS and SSRN returned 403). Group sizes, SEs and survey numbers not read. One country, one subject, one study; no replication found.
agent_relevance: Strongest human evidence that a trusted tool without checks erodes the user's own skill. For an agent: a tool that hands over answers with no derive-and-verify step lowers internal competence. Supports guardrailed tool use.

source: Smart, Clowes and Clark (2025) ChatGPT, extended: large language models and the extended mind, Synthese 205:242
finding: Builds Digital Andy (RAG over Clark's works, gpt-3.5-turbo-1106) and asks if it is an extended system like Otto. Gives no formal test but names two problems that work as criteria: redundancy and agency/control.
numbers: Four conditions: GPTDEFAULT, GPTMODIFIED (no retrieval, same persona prompt), DAPARAGRAPHS, DASECTIONS. Qualitative judging of first responses from a single run on 26 Dec 2023, no scores. GPTDEFAULT did not know 'wideware'; GPTMODIFIED got 'wideware' and 'Otto' right, so the weights already held the facts. Paragraph chunks found Lolo (Clark's cat); section chunks did not.
quote: must have some awareness of Clark's philosophical work
limits: No numbers, one model, first response only. Adams and Aizawa and Rupert are not engaged as rivals (only a 'mark of the cognitive' footnote citing Adams 2010).
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly closed: a usable test. If the store only repeats what the weights hold, the loop is redundant and the extension claim is weak. Test: ablate the store and see whether performance falls.

source: Smart, Clowes and Clark (2025), agency and control, and computational reframing
finding: Second problem: the retrieval call is made by the app, not the LLM, so Digital Andy is passive, unlike Otto who decides to look. They suggest dropping the word cognitive and calling it extended computation if readers object.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Authors say the effect of this difference on the extension claim remains unclear. A tool-calling agent that decides when to retrieve (ReAct, MemGPT) would meet the control condition; Digital Andy as built does not.
agent_relevance: Design implication: let the agent itself decide when to read or write notes (Otto-like), not a fixed pre-retrieval step. Lines up with MemGPT-style self-managed memory (K08).

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Agents copy retrieved records closely when the new query is similar (experience-following). Wrong stored runs then propagate, and adding every run to memory flattens or lowers success. Strict quality filtering keeps improving.
numbers: Four agents (incl. RegAgent, AgentDriver, EHRAgent). Add-all and coarse-LLM-evaluator additions: flat or declining success. Strict selective addition keeps improving, and for AgentDriver passes the ground-truth-retrieval variant after about 2,000 runs. Input-output similarity near Pearson r=1 with memory; lower with fixed memory. Replacing retrieved runs with ground truth gives an immediate gap that grows under add-all.
limits: Headline averages not read (a search summary says about 10% absolute gain; unverified). Simulated task streams, not live deployment.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 2 in part: wrong notes do mislead and the effect is strong. Rule that worked: write a note only after a strong evaluator or human check (verify on write), and delete notes that prove useless when retrieved.

source: Mishra and Mishra (2026) When Does Memory Help? A Cost-Aware Evaluation of Long-Term Memory in Tool-Using LLM Agents (MERIT)
finding: Memory is needed (floor 0.00 without it) but design matters more than presence. Embedding retrieval collapses on updated facts. Overwriting stores and LLM summaries hold up. A hybrid is worse than the fact store alone. Full replay is accurate but never the best value per dollar.
numbers: 23,440 scored episodes, $42.57. Dependent-task success 0.55-1.00 with memory vs 0.00 floor. Hard tier (D1/D2/D3): replay 1.00/0.95/1.00; retrieval 0.70/0.35/0.45; summary 1.00/0.70/1.00; fact store 0.95/0.75/1.00; hybrid 0.80/0.60/0.50. Agents act on a correctly retrieved value only 55% of the time. Swapping an implementation moved success up to 60 points. Replay costs 2.7x tokens; best condition gives 2.7-3.9x marginal utility per dollar. Sonnet 5 spot-check reproduces the pattern.
quote: the hybrid is worse than the fact store alone
limits: Independent authors, small cells (about 10-20 episodes per cell, 3 seeds), GPT-4.1, Haiku 4.5, one Sonnet 5 cell. Memory side held fixed. Opus 4.8 failed the replay control and was not scored.
agent_relevance: Closes much of gap 1 for tool-using tasks: persistent memory beats nothing, replay is the accuracy ceiling but costs 2.7x, overwriting structured notes match it at lower cost. Rule: notes must overwrite, not accumulate.

source: Mishra and Mishra (2026) MERIT, stale-memory harm and provenance
finding: Injected stale records hurt mostly the hybrid store. LLM-based fact extraction ingests corrupted records that a rigid parser rejected. Agents without timestamps average, ask, or pick the stale value.
numbers: Stale-memory harm on D1 at corruption rate 0.3: hybrid +0.25 (Holm p=0.030, the only significant harm). Fact store with LLM extraction +0.20 (raw p=0.013, not significant after Holm) vs regex version 0.05. Contradiction and distractor corruption: small, not significant at pilot scale.
limits: Corruption sweeps beyond one domain left to future work; verification-rate analysis not done. Pilot scale.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 2 partly: stale harm is real but significant in one configuration only. Rule: store timestamps and provenance with every note, overwrite on update, treat extraction as a risk step.

source: Pollertlam and Kornsuwannawit (2026) Beyond the Context Window: Fact-Based Memory vs Long-Context LLMs for Persistent Agents
finding: Full conversation in context beat a Mem0 fact-memory system on factual recall; memory was only competitive on persona consistency. Memory wins on cost after enough turns.
numbers: Accuracy % (memory / long-context GPT-5-mini / long-context GPT-OSS-120B): LoCoMo 57.68 / 92.85 / 81.69; PersonaMem v2 62.48 / 69.75 / 60.50; LongMemEval 49.00 / 82.40 / 48.20. At 100k context, memory becomes cheaper after about 10 turns.
limits: Memory pipeline is GPT-5-nano extraction plus GPT-5-mini reader. Conversational QA, not reasoning with tools. Authors work at a company that sells memory systems.
agent_relevance: Against gap 1: when the context fits, full context is more accurate than lossy extracted notes. A notes file gains by cost and context overflow, not by accuracy at equal tokens. Keep raw records as well as notes.

source: Terranova, Ross and Birch (2025) Evaluating Long-Term Memory for Long-Context Question Answering
finding: On LoCoMo, memory methods use over 90% fewer tokens and often match full context. Which memory works depends on model strength. Full context is best for some models and categories.
numbers: Llama: full context average-F1 rank 1.00 at 23,266 tokens per query; A-Mem 1,306 tokens. GPT-4o-mini: full context 23,132 tokens, rank 3.40, adversarial 52.94; A-Mem 969 tokens, adversarial 77.64; RAG adversarial 64.93 at 3,514 tokens; best variants adversarial 84-93 at about 650-670 tokens. Llama single-hop F1 full 32.45 vs A-Mem 2.12.
limits: Mean F1 with SD over reruns; LoCoMo plus QMSum only; Letta/MemGPT not tested. Memory gains are largest on adversarial (unanswerable) questions, where full context hallucinates.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gaps 1 and 8: at far lower tokens memory is competitive on some categories and better at saying 'not in the record', but not on single-hop recall for weak models.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) PruneTIR: Inference-Time Tool Call Pruning for Effective yet Efficient Tool-Integrated Reasoning
finding: A tool-integrated reasoning method compared with Self-Consistency at matched tokens only slightly beat it on 2 of 3 math sets. At matched budget the tool loop is not a large win.
numbers: Qwen3-8B. AIME24 / AIME25 / BeyondAIME: Self-Consistency 73.3 / 56.7 / 35.0; PruneTIR 72.7 / 60.9 / 35.4 (about 9.5K-10.9K tokens). Tool pruning costs 1.38x base tokens, so SC was set to 2 samples to match.
limits: Math with a code tool; the pruned variant is the authors' own method. I read table lines and the matching note, not the whole paper. Not ReAct with search.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 partly addressed: at roughly matched tokens tool use plus pruning roughly ties self-consistency (-0.6, +4.2, +0.4 points). No clean ReAct vs SC at matched tokens on a modern model found. Stays open.

source: Chen et al. (2026) DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents
finding: Agents repeat tool calls that return identical output. Context compression raises loops. A simple exact-duplicate blocker did not stop agents proposing repeats. Training on loop pairs cut them.
numbers: CodeGym, Qwen3-8B: loop rate 29.0% full history, 57.3% under 4,096-token compression. Looping runs fail 59.5% vs 33.4% loop-free. Duplicate blocker: still proposes an already-executed call in 71.3% of tasks vs 69.8% without blocker. Trace or ledger summaries: still 52.0-62.7% loops. DeLoop DPO: 57.3% to 6.1%, about one third the steps; Qwen3-32B success 37.7% to 44.8%. GRPO loop penalty: 15.0%.
limits: Coding-style environment, small open models plus some Gemini runs. The Reflexion-on-stuck table is garbled in my extraction, so omitted. Blocker result is proposed-call rate, not task success.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 9: repetition is common (29-57% of tasks) and a hard guard does not fix proposals. A repeat guard must also offer a changed action, not only block.

source: Chen et al. (2026) DeLoop, history-record ablation
finding: Removing the record of a past call makes the agent repeat it far more, so agents do use their own log, but only partly.
numbers: Repeat in 3.3% of samples with the record present vs 48.8% with it removed (same action sampled 8 times). Qwen3-8B fails 85% of looping runs vs 68% loop-free; Gemini 3.1 Pro 48% vs 12%.
limits: Single probing setup (Appendix F).
agent_relevance: Supports keeping a visible action log in the scaffold, an external memory that changes behaviour, but it is not sufficient alone.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM)
finding: A shared store of agent trajectories retrieved by other agents raises success and cuts steps. A transactive-memory style system for LLMs, not a test of Wegner's findings.
numbers: ALFWorld: success 47% to 55% (+8.0 points), steps 11.77 to 11.18; with SVMRank reranker 64.3%, steps 10.35. WebArena: 18% to 20%, steps 22.0 to 20.3. Retrieval budget 1 trajectory per call.
limits: Authors' own benchmark runs; WebArena gain small. Retrieval scope ablation shows full-index retrieval (0.2979 success) far below task-type-matched retrieval (0.5985), so unmatched retrieval can hurt.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partial: what carries over from Wegner is retrieving from the right source (task-matched), not from everything. For one agent, index notes by task type.

source: Perrier (2025) Operationalising Extended Cognition: Formal Metrics for Corporate Knowledge and Legal Accountability
finding: Proposes a formal knowledge metric for a system with AI retrieval, combining pipeline cost and statistically validated error rate, with a threshold predicate for 'knows'.
numbers: No empirical numbers in the part I read (abstract and introduction).
limits: Only the first page read; legal-theory framing, no LLM experiment.
agent_relevance: A candidate measurable criterion for gap 5: count a store as part of the agent's knowledge only above a validated reliability threshold. Fits Clark and Chalmers' trusted condition if trust is earned by measured error rate.

source: Baek and Pradel (2026) Automated Table Reproduction via Code Generation (Artisan)
finding: Search summary: removing the format tool lowered successful reproductions from 44 to 35 and raised copied-results scripts from 2 to 9. The paper has a 'w/o Format Tool' ablation row.
numbers: 44 to 35 successes, 2 to 9 copied-results scripts (from search summary; not verified in the table).
limits: Coding-adjacent, 60 tasks. I saw only the ablation row label.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for gap 3: an interface constraint changes agent behaviour, but it is still a code task. No non-code reasoning interface study with numbers found. Gap 3 stays open.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies
finding: Search summary: with compute matched, chain of thought plus self-consistency is very competitive and strategy rankings change once cost is counted.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Snippet only. 2024, not tool agents. An ACL 2026 SRW paper extends budget-aware evaluation to tool agents (not opened).
agent_relevance: Supports the caution that tool-loop gains in K05 and K07 need token-matched controls.

source: Mnemon, Memanto and MemUse papers (2026): Letta/MemGPT scores on LoCoMo, as described in a search summary
finding: Search summary: re-evaluations by rival system authors put Letta at 74.0% (full context 72.9%) on LoCoMo in one paper, 77.12% with about 14.2k context tokens in another, and 61.4% on a different task.
limits: Snippet only; rival authors; different reader models. Not independent in a strict sense.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no clean independent replication of MemGPT's own numbers found; MemGPT-style memory sits near full-context level on LoCoMo, not far above it.
